opus-5.5.text:
Well, in some ways it has succeeded beyond what I expected, and in other ways it's still very far from where I want it to be.

When I started pushing self-supervised learning, around 2016 or so with the "cake" analogy, where self-supervised learning is the bulk of the cake, supervised learning is the icing, and reinforcement learning is the cherry, a lot of people were skeptical. The dominant paradigm was supervised learning: label a lot of data, train a big convolutional net, done. My argument was that humans and animals don't learn that way. A baby learns an enormous amount about how the world works just by observation, with almost no labels and very little interaction. So the big question was: how do we get machines to learn like that?

The success came first, and most spectacularly, in language. Large language models are trained with self-supervised learning: you take a text, you mask or remove some words, and you train the system to predict them. That works extremely well for text, and it has completely transformed natural language processing. So in that sense the vision was vindicated, probably more dramatically than most people expected.

But the reason it works so well for text is that text is discrete. You have a finite vocabulary, so you can produce a probability distribution over all possible next tokens. You can handle uncertainty. When you try to apply the same idea to video, to the real world, predicting the next frame at the pixel level, it basically doesn't work. The world is not completely predictable, and there are infinitely many plausible futures. If you train a system to predict pixels, you get blurry predictions, because it averages over all the possibilities. We spent years trying to make that work, and it doesn't.

So that's where I've moved toward what I call joint embedding architectures, JEPA, Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture. Instead of predicting every detail of the input, you learn an abstract representation and make predictions in that representation space. The system can then ignore the details that are inherently unpredictable, like exactly how the leaves on a tree move, and focus on what matters. We've had some quite encouraging results with I-JEPA and V-JEPA on images and video.

Where it falls short of what I hoped is this: we still don't have systems that learn world models the way a cat or a young child does. A four-year-old has seen, through vision alone, about as much data as the largest LLMs are trained on in text. And yet that child understands intuitive physics, object permanence, cause and effect, things our AI systems still don't really grasp. LLMs can manipulate language impressively, but they don't understand the physical world, they can't really plan, and they don't have persistent memory or reasoning in the true sense.

So, the short answer: self-supervised learning has won the argument, everybody uses it now. But the next step, learning world models from sensory input like video, so that machines can plan and reason, is still ahead of us. That's what I think the next few years of AI research will be about, and it's not going to come from just scaling up LLMs.

r001.rationale: The response says babies learn how the world works through observation and frames the goal as getting machines to learn that way.

r002.rationale: It describes making predictions in an abstract representation space, but does not say those learned representations are used as inputs for downstream tasks.

r003.rationale: It highlights self-supervised learning’s especially dramatic success in language and contrasts it with unsuccessful pixel-level prediction for video.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's funny, because in some ways it's exceeded what I hoped for, and in other ways it's fallen short of what I actually wanted.

If you go back ten, fifteen years, I was going around saying that the cake is self-supervised learning, the icing is supervised learning, and the cherry on top is reinforcement learning. People laughed at that. The idea was that the vast majority of what humans and animals learn is learned by observation, not by being told the answer, and not by trial and error with rewards. So if we wanted machines to learn anything like the way we learn, most of the learning had to be self-supervised.

And then it happened. In natural language, it happened in a big way. You take a piece of text, you remove some words, you train a giant neural net to predict the missing words, and you get all of the large language models we have today. That is self-supervised learning. It worked far better than almost anyone expected, including me. In vision, it took longer, but we got there too with things like joint embedding methods, DINO, and so on. So the bet paid off, and I would say it's now the dominant paradigm.

But here is where it falls short. The success in language came from a trick that works for text and does not work for the physical world. Text is discrete. You can predict a probability distribution over a dictionary of words. You cannot do that for video. The world is continuous and mostly unpredictable in its details, and if you try to predict every pixel of the next frame, you waste all your capacity on things that are irrelevant and you end up with a blurry average. We tried that for years. It didn't work.

So what I actually wanted from self-supervised learning was not a better autocomplete. I wanted machines that learn how the world works by watching it, the way a baby does in the first few months of life. Intuitive physics, object permanence, the fact that if I push this thing it will move. That's the hard part, and the LLM recipe does not get us there. What I think gets us there is learning to predict in an abstract representation space rather than in input space, which is the whole idea behind JEPA, the joint embedding predictive architecture. You predict the representation of the future, not the future itself, and you let the system throw away the unpredictable details.

So if you ask me how it compares to the original hope, I'd say we got the easy half faster than expected, and the hard half, the world model half, is where I've spent the last several years, and where I think the next real progress is going to come from. I'm actually more optimistic about it now than I was a few years ago, because we finally have architectures where it's not just a hope, it's starting to work.

r001.rationale: LeCun says he wanted machines to learn how the world works by watching it, like a baby.

r002.rationale: The response describes predicting future representations, but does not say those learned representations are used as inputs for downstream tasks.

r003.rationale: It says self-supervised learning in language worked far better than expected, while attempts to predict video frames failed and vision took longer.

astra-6.text:
It has been very successful, but in a somewhat different way from what I originally hoped. The idea was that a system could learn useful representations from enormous amounts of raw data, without humans having to label everything. That part has worked remarkably well, particularly in language. Predicting missing words, or predicting the next word, turned out to provide a very powerful training signal.

What I hoped, though, was that this would lead us toward systems that understand the world more like humans and animals do. And there, we still have a lot of work to do. Learning the regularities of text is not the same as learning how the physical world works—what happens when you take an action, what is predictable, what is uncertain.

So I would distinguish the success of self-supervised learning as a principle from the question of whether we have the right architectures and objectives. The principle is very powerful. But I think we need systems that learn to predict in an abstract representation space, where they can ignore irrelevant details, rather than trying to predict every pixel or every possible detail of an observation. That is the direction that interests me: learning models of the world that can support reasoning and planning.

r001.rationale: The response says LeCun hoped systems would learn to understand how the physical world works from raw, unlabeled data, which conveys learning about the world through observation.

r002.rationale: It discusses representations learned through prediction and says world models could support reasoning and planning, but does not describe using those representations as inputs for downstream tasks.

r003.rationale: It identifies language as a particularly successful area, but does not mention video or that this success differed from the video domain LeCun had pursued.

sol-6.1.text:
It has been very successful, but I think we’re still some distance from the original ambition. The idea was that a machine should learn how the world works by observing it, without someone having to label everything. In language, self-supervised learning has worked spectacularly well: you hide or predict parts of the text, and the system learns representations that are useful for all kinds of tasks.

But learning from text is only part of the problem. We’d like systems that can watch the world, understand what’s happening, predict the consequences of actions, and use those predictions to plan. Video is much more difficult because there are many possible things that can happen, and a lot of detail that is irrelevant or impossible to predict.

So I’m encouraged by the progress, but the goal was never just to build systems that generate fluent language. It was to get machines to acquire something like common sense. I think self-supervised learning is an essential ingredient, but we still have substantial work to do.

r001.rationale: The response says the idea was for machines to learn how the world works by observing it without everything being labeled.

r002.rationale: It says prediction produces representations useful for many tasks, but does not clearly say those representations are used as inputs for learning downstream tasks.

r003.rationale: It describes strong results in language and greater difficulty with video, but does not identify the language success as unexpected or say video was the domain LeCun had pursued.
